Chapter Two: The Spread of Drug Laws and the Rise of Organized Crime.
As the United States ramped up its war on drugs, it wasn’t just an American story anymore. The pressure quickly spilled over borders—thanks to international treaties and political maneuvering—pushing other countries to adopt the same hardline approach. But here’s the thing: in so many of these places, substances like coca leaves or opium weren’t just drugs. They were part of daily life, woven into tradition and culture for centuries.
Suddenly, these age-old practices became crimes overnight. Imagine entire communities waking up to find their way of life declared illegal. That’s exactly what happened. And for many, it wasn’t just about breaking the law—it was about survival.
Take Mexico, for example. When the crackdown intensified, opportunities opened up for anyone willing to take risks outside the law. Smugglers and traffickers adapted fast, creating networks that could move mountains of drugs across borders. The profits? They were huge. Sure, the dangers were real, but for a lot of people, the alternative—staying poor and hungry—seemed even worse.
Picture a young man in a small rural village, watching neighbors get swept up in this new world of smuggling. At first, he tries to find honest work, hoping things will turn around. But as jobs vanish and the local economy collapses, he faces a gut-wrenching choice. Support his family by following the same path—or let them go without. The money is tempting, but every day comes with risk. Friends disappear without warning, and violence is always lurking in the background. Still, when you’re staring down poverty, it’s hard to walk away.
The rise of organized crime changed everything. Rival groups battled for control, and innocent people often got caught in the middle. Corruption wormed its way through police forces and local governments, making it tough to know who, if anyone, you could trust. In some towns, drug cartels became the real power, leaving officials helpless to do anything about it.
Meanwhile, back in the United States, the impact of prohibition was getting harder to ignore. Prisons started overflowing, mostly with people locked up for drug-related offenses. And these weren’t seasoned criminals—many were just everyday folks caught in a system that showed little mercy. Families were torn apart, and the cycle of poverty and incarceration got even deeper.
Even as the evidence piled up that the War on Drugs wasn’t working, politicians kept doubling down. Tougher laws, harsher penalties—the belief that drugs could be wiped out by force was still incredibly powerful. But on the ground, the reality looked very different.
For people living under the shadow of the drug war, hope was hard to come by. But here’s a glimmer: a few started to wonder if there might be another way. Instead of focusing on punishment, they began asking deeper questions—like, why do people turn to drugs in the first place? And what if understanding those reasons could lead to real change?
